results.title: Kourovka Problem 17.116 (two-generated direct powers of simple groups)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement, in the form of its resolution, that for every non-abelian finite simple group $G$ there is a natural number $n$ with $n^2 > 4|G|$, that is, $n > 2\sqrt{|G|}$, such that the direct power $G^n$ is generated by two elements. The problem is due to A. Erfanian and J. Wiegold.

results.title: Maróti–Tamburini bound for two-generated direct powers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every non-abelian finite simple group $G$ there is a natural number $n$ with $n^2 > 4|G|$, that is, $n > 2\sqrt{|G|}$, such that the direct power $G^n$ is generated by two elements. This answers Kourovka Problem 17.116 positively.

results.title: Odd part
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n \ge 1$, the odd part $\operatorname{od}(n)$ is $n / 2^{\nu_2(n)}$, where $2^{\nu_2(n)}$ is the largest power of $2$ dividing $n$; it is the odd factor of $n$ left after removing that power of $2$. For $n = 0$ the definition gives $\operatorname{od}(0) = 0$.

results.title: Odd part as a quotient by a power of two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary:
For every natural number $n$, $\mathrm{od}(n) = n / 2^{
u_2(n)}$, where $\mathrm{od}(n)$ is the odd part of $n$ and $
u_2(n)$ is the exponent of $2$ in the prime factorization of $n$, with $
u_2(0) = 0$.

results.title: Odd-range product
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $l$ and $m$, the odd-range product $\operatorname{odpr}(l, m)$ is the product of the odd natural numbers $j$ with $l \le j \le m$; it equals $1$ when there are none.

results.title: Odd-range product as a filtered product
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $l$ and $m$, the odd-range product $\operatorname{odpr}(l, m)$ equals the product $\prod j$ over the odd natural numbers $j$ in the closed interval $[l, m]$.

results.title: Odd product block
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $m$, the odd product block $h(m)$ is the product of the odd integers $j$ with $2^{m-1}+1 \le j \le 2^m-1$. In particular $h(0) = h(1) = 1$, as empty products.

results.title: Odd product block as an odd-range product
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $m$, the odd product block $h(m)$ equals $\operatorname{odpr}(2^{m-1}+1, 2^m-1)$, the product of the odd integers $j$ with $2^{m-1}+1 \le j \le 2^m-1$.

results.title: Unstable bits

results.title: Dyadic upper half interval

results.summary: For a natural number $e$, $I_e$ is the finite set of natural numbers $i$ with $2^{e-1} < i \le 2^e$, where $e - 1$ is truncated subtraction, so that $I_0$ is empty.

results.title: Integer multiset of a finite set of naturals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $s$ of natural numbers, its integer multiset is the multiset of integers obtained by sending each element $n \in s$ to $n$ viewed as an integer, so each element of $s$ occurs exactly once.

results.title: Cardinality of the integer multiset
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite set $s$ of natural numbers, the integer multiset of $s$ has the same number of elements, counted with multiplicity, as $s$.

results.title: Reversed elementary symmetric functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let $S$ be a finite multiset of elements of $R$ with $n$ elements counted with multiplicity, and let $i$ be a natural number. Here $n - i$ is truncated subtraction, so $\hat\sigma_i(S) = \sigma_0(S) = 1$ whenever $i \ge n$.

results.title: Unfolding the reversed elementary symmetric function

results.title: Odd double factorial below a power of two

results.title: Doubly ruled graphs are planes or hyperbolic paraboloids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a real-valued function of two real variables whose graph is doubly ruled; no continuity of $f$ is assumed. Then there are real numbers $a, b, c, d, e, g$ such that $f(x, y) = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 + dx + ey + g$ for all real $x$ and $y$, and either $a = b = c = 0$ (the graph is a plane) or $b^2 - 4ac > 0$ (the graph is a hyperbolic paraboloid).

results.title: Types of the simply typed lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Fix a type $B$ of base types. The types over $B$ are generated by the grammar $T ::= b \mid \mathsf{Unit} \mid T_1 \to T_2 \mid \mathsf{Ref}\,T$ with $b \in B$: base types, the unit type, function types, and types $\mathsf{Ref}\,T$ of reference cells holding values of type $T$.

results.title: Terms of the simply typed lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Fix a type $B$ of base types. The terms are generated by: variables, given as de Bruijn indices $x \in \mathbb{N}$; abstractions $\lambda{:}T.\,t$, where $T$ is a type over $B$ and $t$ is a term in which index $0$ refers to the abstraction's parameter; applications $t_1\,t_2$; the unit value $\mathsf{unit}$; store locations $l \in \mathbb{N}$; allocations $\mathsf{ref}\,t$; dereferences $!t$; and assignments…

results.title: Values of the simply typed lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A term is a value if and only if it is an abstraction $\lambda{:}T.\,t$, the unit value $\mathsf{unit}$, or a store location $l$.

results.title: Lifting a renaming under a binder in the lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a renaming $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of de Bruijn indices, its lift is the renaming that sends $0$ to $0$ and each $x + 1$ to $\rho(x) + 1$.

results.title: Renaming the variables of a term
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a renaming $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of de Bruijn indices, renaming a term by $\rho$ replaces each variable $x$ by $\rho(x)$; renames the body of an abstraction $\lambda{:}T.\,t$ by the lift of $\rho$ (which sends $0$ to $0$ and each $x + 1$ to $\rho(x) + 1$), keeping the type annotation $T$; leaves the unit value and store locations unchanged; and acts componentwise on applications, allocations,…

results.title: Lifting a substitution under a binder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a substitution $\sigma$ assigning a term to each de Bruijn index, its lift is the substitution that sends $0$ to the variable $0$ and each $x + 1$ to the term $\sigma(x)$ renamed by $n \mapsto n + 1$, that is, with every free variable raised by one.

results.title: Parallel substitution in a term
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a substitution $\sigma$ assigning a term to each de Bruijn index, substituting $\sigma$ into a term replaces each variable $x$ by $\sigma(x)$; substitutes into the body of an abstraction $\lambda{:}T.\,t$ the lift of $\sigma$ (which sends $0$ to the variable $0$ and each $x + 1$ to $\sigma(x)$ with every free variable raised by one), keeping the type annotation $T$; leaves the unit value and store locations…

results.title: Single-variable substitution at index zero
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a term $s$, the single-variable substitution for $s$ sends the de Bruijn index $0$ to $s$ and each index $x + 1$ to the variable $x$.

results.title: Substitution of a term for variable zero
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For terms $t$ and $s$, the instantiation of $t$ by $s$ applies to $t$ the parallel substitution that sends the de Bruijn index $0$ to $s$ and each index $x + 1$ to the variable $x$. Thus the free occurrences of variable $0$ in $t$ are replaced by $s$, with the free variables of $s$ raised by the number of binders crossed, and every other free variable of $t$ is lowered by one.

results.title: Store
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A store $\mu$ is a finite list of terms; each location $l$ less than the length of $\mu$ holds the term $\mu[l]$, the entry of $\mu$ at index $l$.

results.title: One-step evaluation with references
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: One step of call-by-value evaluation $t \mid \mu \to t' \mid \mu'$, from a term $t$ with a store $\mu$ to a term $t'$ with a store $\mu'$, is the least relation closed under the following rules, in which $v$, $v_1$ and $v_2$ are values. If $t \mid \mu \to t' \mid \mu'$, then $t\,t_2 \mid \mu \to t'\,t_2 \mid \mu'$, $v_1\,t \mid \mu \to v_1\,t' \mid \mu'$, $\mathsf{ref}\,t \mid \mu \to \mathsf{ref}\,t' \mid \mu'$,…

results.title: Multi-step evaluation with references
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The relation $t \mid \mu \to^* t' \mid \mu'$ holds when the configuration $(t, \mu)$ reaches $(t', \mu')$ in zero or more evaluation steps; that is, it is the reflexive-transitive closure of one-step evaluation on pairs of a term and a store.

results.title: Values do not step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $v$ is a value, then there are no stores $\mu$, $\mu'$ and term $t'$ such that the configuration $(v, \mu)$ steps to $(t', \mu')$: values are normal forms.

results.title: Determinism of evaluation with references
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a configuration $(t, \mu)$ steps to $(t_1, \mu_1)$ and also to $(t_2, \mu_2)$, then $t_1 = t_2$ and $\mu_1 = \mu_2$.

results.title: Renaming respects pointwise equality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\rho, \rho' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be renamings of de Bruijn variables with $\rho(x) = \rho'(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, renaming $t$ by $\rho$ gives the same term as renaming $t$ by $\rho'$.

results.title: Renaming by the identity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, renaming the de Bruijn variables of $t$ by the identity map of $\mathbb{N}$ gives back $t$.

results.title: Composition of renamings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all renamings $\rho, \rho' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of de Bruijn variables and every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, renaming $t$ by $\rho$ and then renaming the result by $\rho'$ gives the same term as renaming $t$ by the composite $\rho' \circ \rho$.

results.title: Substitution respects pointwise equality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma, \sigma'$ be parallel substitutions, each sending every de Bruijn index to a term of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, with $\sigma(x) = \sigma'(x)$ for every $x \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for every term $t$, applying $\sigma$ to $t$ gives the same term as applying $\sigma'$ to $t$.

results.title: Substitution by variables is the identity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every term $t$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, applying the parallel substitution that sends each de Bruijn index $x$ to the variable term $x$ gives back $t$.

results.title: Renaming then substituting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a renaming of de Bruijn variables, $\sigma$ a parallel substitution sending each index to a term of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, and $t$ a term. Renaming $t$ by $\rho$ and then applying $\sigma$ gives the same term as applying the substitution $\sigma \circ \rho$ to $t$.

results.title: Substituting then renaming
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a renaming of de Bruijn variables, $\sigma$ a parallel substitution sending each index to a term of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, and $t$ a term. Applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and then renaming the result by $\rho$ gives the same term as applying to $t$ the substitution that sends each index $x$ to the renaming of $\sigma(x)$ by $\rho$.

results.title: Composition of substitutions in the lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all parallel substitutions $\sigma, \tau$, each sending every de Bruijn index to a term of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, and every term $t$, applying $\sigma$ to $t$ and then $\tau$ to the result gives the same term as applying to $t$ the substitution that sends each index $x$ to the result of applying $\tau$ to $\sigma(x)$.

results.title: Instantiating a shifted term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all terms $t$ and $s$ of the simply typed lambda calculus with references, shift every free de Bruijn variable of $t$ up by one (rename by $x \mapsto x + 1$), then instantiate the result with $s$, replacing variable $0$ by $s$ and lowering every other variable $x + 1$ to $x$. The outcome is $t$.

results.title: Well-typed stores
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and $S$ a store typing. A store $\mu$, a list of terms whose entry at index $l$ is the contents of location $l$, is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$, written $\Gamma \mid S \vdash \mu$, when $\mu$ and $S$ have the same length and, for every location $l$ less than this length, the entry of $\mu$ at $l$ is a value that has, under $\Gamma$ and $S$, the type that $S$ assigns to $l$.

results.title: Well-typed stores hold a typed value at every location
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a typing context, $S$ a store typing, and $\mu$ a store (a list of terms, whose entry at index $l$ is the contents of location $l$) that is well typed, $\Gamma \mid S \vdash \mu$. If $S$ assigns type $T$ to location $l$, then $\mu$ has an entry $v$ at location $l$, $v$ is a value, and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : T$.

results.title: Canonical forms for function types
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context $\Gamma$ and store typing $S$, if $v$ is a value and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : T_1 \to T_2$, then $v$ is an abstraction $\lambda{:}T_1.\, t$ with parameter type $T_1$, for some body $t$.

results.title: Canonical forms for reference types
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context $\Gamma$ and store typing $S$, if $v$ is a value and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : \mathrm{Ref}\, T$, then $v$ is a location $l$ to which $S$ assigns type $T$.

results.title: Canonical forms for the unit type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every context $\Gamma$ and store typing $S$, if $v$ is a value and $\Gamma \mid S \vdash v : \mathrm{Unit}$, then $v = \mathtt{unit}$.

results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Renaming preserves typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be variable contexts, $S$ a store typing, and $\rho : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ a renaming of variable indices such that whenever $\Gamma$ assigns type $A$ to variable $x$, $\Delta$ assigns type $A$ to variable $\rho(x)$. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the term obtained from $t$ by renaming its variables by $\rho$ has type $T$ under $\Delta$ and $S$.

results.title: Weakening of typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a term $t$ has type $T$ in a variable context $\Gamma$ under a store typing $S$, then for every type $A$, the term obtained from $t$ by shifting each free de Bruijn variable up by one has type $T$ under $S$ in the context obtained from $\Gamma$ by adding $A$ in front as variable $0$.

results.title: Parallel substitution preserves typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be variable contexts, $S$ a store typing, and $\sigma$ a substitution sending each variable index to a term, such that whenever $\Gamma$ assigns type $A$ to variable $x$, the term $\sigma(x)$ has type $A$ under $\Delta$ and $S$. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the term obtained from $t$ by applying $\sigma$ has type $T$ under $\Delta$ and $S$.

results.title: Substitution lemma for the lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and $S$ a store typing. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $S$ and the context that extends $\Gamma$ by a new innermost variable (index $0$) of type $A$, and a term $s$ has type $A$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then substituting $s$ for variable $0$ in $t$ (and lowering every other variable by one) gives a term of type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$.

results.title: Store-typing weakening
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and let $S$ and $S'$ be store typings such that $S$ is a prefix of $S'$. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S'$.

results.title: Retyping a well-typed store under an extended store typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context, let $S$ and $S'$ be store typings such that $S$ is a prefix of $S'$, and let $\mu$ be a store that is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$. Then $\mu$ and $S$ have the same length, and for every location $l$ less than this length, the entry of $\mu$ at $l$ is a value that has, under $\Gamma$ and $S'$, the type that $S$ assigns to $l$.

results.title: Allocation preserves store typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context, $S$ a store typing and $\mu$ a store that is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$. If $v$ is a value of type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the store obtained by appending $v$ at the end of $\mu$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and the store typing obtained by appending $T$ at the end of $S$.

results.title: Assignment preserves store typing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the store $\mu$ be well typed under the variable context $\Gamma$ and the store typing $S$, and let $l$ be a location to which $S$ assigns the type $T$. If $v$ is a value of type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, then the store obtained from $\mu$ by overwriting the entry at $l$ with $v$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$.

results.title: Preservation for the lambda calculus with references
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and $S$ a store typing. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, the store $\mu$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$, and $t$ with store $\mu$ takes one evaluation step to $t'$ with store $\mu'$, then there is a store typing $S'$ having $S$ as a prefix such that $t'$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S'$ and $\mu'$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S'$.

results.title: Preservation for multi-step evaluation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a variable context and $S$ a store typing. If a term $t$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S$, the store $\mu$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S$, and $t$ with store $\mu$ evaluates in zero or more steps to $t'$ with store $\mu'$, then there is a store typing $S'$ having $S$ as a prefix such that $t'$ has type $T$ under $\Gamma$ and $S'$ and $\mu'$ is well typed under $\Gamma$ and $S'$.

results.title: Type safety
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a store typing, $T$ a type, $t$ a term of type $T$ in the empty variable context under $S$, and $\mu$ a store that is well typed under $S$ in the empty context. If the configuration $(t, \mu)$ evaluates in zero or more steps to $(t', \mu')$, then $t'$ is a value or $(t', \mu')$ takes a step to some configuration $(t'', \mu'')$. So a closed term that is well typed in a well-typed store never reaches a…

results.title: Type safety from the empty store
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A closed term typed under the empty store typing, run from the empty store, never gets stuck: every term it reaches in zero or more steps, together with the store reached alongside it, is a value or can take a further step.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `pick` is a greedy backward-selection rule for `g`: from a nonempty remaining set `R` it masks a feature `i ∈ R` maximizing `g (R.erase i)`.

results.title: Existence of greedy backward-selection rules

results.title: Backward-selection chain of remaining feature sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Backward selection: the list of remaining sets `R₀ = R, R₁, …, ∅`, where `R_{t+1}` is `R_t` with the feature chosen by `pick` masked.

results.title: FindSIS procedure for sufficient input subsets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `FindSIS`: un-mask features in reverse order of masking (start from `∅`) and return the first set on which the prediction reaches the threshold, or `none`. The paper's procedure does not test `∅` itself; the two agree whenever `g ∅ < τ`, the case the paper considers.

results.title: Backward-selection chain at the empty set

results.title: Sets in the backward-selection chain are subsets of the start
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Starting set begins the backward-selection chain

results.title: FindSIS returns a set when the start reaches the threshold

results.title: FindSIS returns a sufficient subset of the features

results.title: Proposition 1 (second part)

results.title: Minimality of FindSIS for monotone set functions

results.title: Comparator network
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A comparator network on $n$ wires is a finite list of pairs $(i, j)$ of wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, each pair standing for the comparator $(i, j)$; the comparators are applied in list order.

results.title: Comparator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order, let $n$ be a natural number, and let $v$ assign a value $v(k) \in \alpha$ to each wire $k \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. For wires $i$ and $j$, the comparator $(i, j)$ sends $v$ to the assignment that has $\min(v(i), v(j))$ on wire $i$, $\max(v(i), v(j))$ on wire $j$ when $j \ne i$, and $v(k)$ on every other wire $k$.

results.title: Running a comparator network
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. The output of a comparator network on an assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each of its $n$ wires is obtained by starting from $v$ and applying the comparators of the network one after another, in list order.

results.title: Networks that sort
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A comparator network on $n$ wires sorts inputs over a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ if, for every input $v$ assigning a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of running the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order: for all wires $i \le j$, the output value on wire $i$ is at most the output value on wire $j$.

results.title: Comparators commute with monotone maps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be linear orders, let $f : \alpha \to \beta$ be monotone, and let $n$ be a natural number. For all wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the comparator $(i, j)$ applied to $f \circ v$ gives $f \circ w$, where $w$ is the output of the comparator $(i, j)$ on $v$.

results.title: Networks commute with monotone maps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be linear orders and let $f : \alpha \to \beta$ be monotone. For every comparator network on $n$ wires and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of the network on $f \circ v$ is $f \circ w$, where $w$ is the output of the network on $v$.

results.title: A comparator permutes its inputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order and let $n$ be a natural number. For all wires $i, j \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the wires such that the output of the comparator $(i, j)$ on $v$ is $v \circ \sigma$.

results.title: The output of a comparator network is a permutation of its input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For every comparator network on $n$ wires and every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, there is a permutation $\sigma$ of the wires such that the output of the network on $v$ is $v \circ \sigma$.

results.title: The 0-1 principle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The 0-1 principle (CLRS Theorem 27.2): a network that sorts every Boolean input sorts every input over every linear order.

results.title: Boolean sorting test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Boolean sorting test of a comparator network on $n$ wires returns true exactly when, for every assignment $v$ of a Boolean value to each wire, the output $w$ of the network on $v$ satisfies $w(i) \le w(j)$ for all wires $i \le j$, where $\mathrm{false} < \mathrm{true}$.

results.title: The Boolean sorting test is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A comparator network passes the Boolean sorting test if and only if it sorts inputs over the Booleans, that is, for every assignment of a Boolean value to each wire, the output of the network is monotone in the wire order.

results.title: A network that passes the Boolean sorting test sorts over every linear order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a comparator network on $n$ wires passes the Boolean sorting test, then for every linear order $\alpha$ it sorts inputs over $\alpha$: for every assignment $v$ of a value in $\alpha$ to each wire, the output of the network on $v$ is monotone in the wire order.

results.title: Spread of a Boolean input
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Boolean input $v$ on $n$ wires, the spread of $v$ is the input with natural-number values whose value on wire $i < n$ is $n + i$ if $v(i)$ is true and $i$ if $v(i)$ is false.

results.title: A Boolean input is a threshold of its spread
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Boolean input $v$ on $n$ wires, applying the threshold map that sends a natural number $k$ to true if $n \le k$ and to false otherwise to the spread of $v$ gives back $v$: for every wire $i$, the spread of $v$ at $i$ is at least $n$ exactly when $v(i)$ is true.

results.title: Sorting distinct inputs suffices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A network that sorts every input with distinct natural values sorts every input over every linear order.

results.title: Rank among the values of an input
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a map $w$ from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the natural numbers and an index $i < n$, the rank of $w(i)$ among the values of $w$ is the number of indices $j < n$ with $w(j) < w(i)$. It is less than $n$, so it is again an index in $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

results.title: The ranking permutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an injective map $w$ from $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ to the natural numbers, the ranking permutation of $w$ is the permutation of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ that sends each $i$ to the rank of $w(i)$ among the values of $w$, that is, to the number of indices $j$ with $w(j) < w(i)$. Since $w$ is injective, this map is a bijection.

results.title: The permutation principle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A comparator network on $n$ wires that sorts each of the $n!$ permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, viewed as the input whose value on wire $i$ is $\sigma(i)$, sorts every input over every linear order.

With move bound $k + 1$ the player to move wins at $(A, B)$ exactly when some legal…

results.title: First player wins Snort
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. In Snort on $G$ the two players alternately colour a vertex that is not yet coloured and is not adjacent to any vertex coloured by the opponent, and a player with no legal move loses. The first player wins Snort on $G$ when the player who moves first has a winning strategy from the position in which no vertex is coloured.

results.title: Second-player win in Snort
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. In Snort on $G$, two players alternately colour a vertex of $G$ that is not yet coloured, each with their own colour, and a player may not colour a vertex adjacent to a vertex of the opponent's colour; a player with no legal move loses. The second player wins Snort on $G$ if, starting from the position in which no vertex is coloured, the player who moves first has no winning…

results.title: Snort response pairs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In Snort on a finite graph $G$, a pair $(u, v)$ of vertices is a response pair if $u \neq v$, $u$ and $v$ are not adjacent (so the first player colouring $u$ and the second answering $v$ is legal), and the first player, now to move, loses from the position in which the first player has coloured $u$ and the second player has coloured $v$.

results.title: Oppositions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An opposition of a graph $G$ is an automorphism $f$ of $G$ such that for every vertex $v$, $f(f(v)) = v$, $f(v) \neq v$, and $f(v)$ is not adjacent to $v$; that is, an involutive automorphism moving every vertex outside its closed neighbourhood.

results.title: Opposable graphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A graph $G$ is opposable if it has an opposition: an automorphism $f$ of $G$ such that for every vertex $v$, $f(f(v)) = v$, $f(v) \neq v$, and $f(v)$ is not adjacent to $v$.

results.title: Almost opposable graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A graph $G$ is almost opposable if there are a vertex $u$ and a set $S$ of vertices with $u \in S \subseteq N[u]$, where $N[u]$ is the closed neighbourhood of $u$ ($u$ together with its neighbours), such that the subgraph $G - S$ induced on the vertices outside $S$ is opposable.

results.title: Compatibly almost opposable graphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A graph $G$ is compatibly almost opposable if there are a vertex $u$, a set $S$ of vertices with $u \in S \subseteq N[u]$ (the closed neighbourhood of $u$), an automorphism $\alpha$ of $G$ with $\alpha(\alpha(v)) = v$ for every vertex $v$, and an opposition $f$ of the subgraph $G - S$ induced on the vertices outside $S$, such that $\alpha(x) = f(x)$ for every vertex $x \notin S$.

results.title: Opposition matchings
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a graph. A subgraph $M$ of $K$ is an opposition matching of $K$ if it is a perfect matching of $K$ and for any two distinct edges $ab$ and $cd$ of $M$, $ac \in E(K) \iff bd \in E(K)$ and $ad \in E(K) \iff bc \in E(K)$.

results.title: Graph product given by a Boolean formula
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs with vertex sets $V$ and $W$, and let $\varphi$ be a Boolean function of four Boolean arguments. The product $G \varphi H$ is the graph on $V \times W$ in which two distinct vertices $(g_1, h_1)$ and $(g_2, h_2)$ are adjacent exactly when $\varphi(g_1 g_2 \in E(G), h_1 h_2 \in E(H), g_1 = g_2, h_1 = h_2)$ is true.

results.title: Strong product of graphs
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For simple graphs $G$ on $V$ and $H$ on $W$, the strong product $G \boxtimes H$ is the simple graph on $V \times W$ in which $(g_1, h_1)$ and $(g_2, h_2)$ are adjacent if and only if $g_1 = g_2$ and $h_1 h_2$ is an edge of $H$, or $g_1 g_2$ is an edge of $G$ and $h_1 = h_2$, or $g_1 g_2$ is an edge of $G$ and $h_1 h_2$ is an edge of $H$.

results.title: Firework of a graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a graph $G$, vertices $u$ and $v$ of $G$ and a natural number $n$, the $n$-firework of $G$ at $(u, v)$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by adding $2n$ new vertices, $n$ of which are adjacent only to $u$ and the other $n$ adjacent only to $v$.

results.title: Strong grid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and natural numbers $n_0, \dots, n_{k-1}$, the $k$-dimensional strong grid $P_{n_0} \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes P_{n_{k-1}}$ is the simple graph whose vertices are the tuples $(x_0, \dots, x_{k-1})$ of integers with $0 \le x_i < n_i$ for each $i$, in which two vertices $x$ and $y$ are adjacent if and only if $x \ne y$ and $|x_i - y_i| \le 1$ for every $i$.

results.title: Cartesian grid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and side lengths $n_1, \dots, n_k \in \mathbb{N}$, the $k$-dimensional Cartesian grid has as vertices the tuples $(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ of integers with $0 \le x_i < n_i$ for each $i$, and two tuples are adjacent when they differ in exactly one coordinate, and there by exactly one. It is the Cartesian product $P_{n_1} \square \cdots \square P_{n_k}$ of the paths $P_{n_i}$ on $n_i$ vertices.

results.title: King's graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the king's graph of the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two distinct pairs $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when $|i - i'| \le 1$ and $|j - j'| \le 1$.

results.title: Knight's graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the knight's graph of the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two pairs $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when either $|i - i'| = 1$ and $|j - j'| = 2$, or $|i - i'| = 2$ and $|j - j'| = 1$.

results.title: Bishop's graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the bishop's graph on the $n \times m$ board has as vertices the cells $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, and two distinct cells $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when they lie on a common diagonal, that is, when $|i - i'| = |j - j'|$.

results.title: Queen's graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, the queen's graph of the $n \times m$ board is the simple graph whose vertices are the pairs $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i < n$ and $0 \le j < m$, in which two distinct pairs $(i, j)$ and $(i', j')$ are adjacent when $i = i'$, or $j = j'$, or $|i - i'| = |j - j'|$; that is, when they share a row, a column or a diagonal.

results.title: Snort on two vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The first player wins Snort on the complete graph $K_2$, and the second player wins Snort on the graph with two vertices and no edges.

results.title: Snort on the $2 \times 2$ queen's and rook's graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The first player wins Snort on the queen's graph of the $2 \times 2$ board (the Peaceable Queens game), and the second player wins Snort on the rook's graph of the $2 \times 2$ board (the Peaceable Rooks game).

results.title: Fireworks preserve second-player wins in Snort
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and let $(u, v)$ be a response pair of $G$ whose distance in $G$ is at least $3$ (infinite distance, when $u$ and $v$ lie in different components, is allowed). results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $N$ there is a tree $T$ on $n \ge N$ vertices such that the second player wins Snort on $T$.

results.title: Strong products of compatibly almost opposable graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $G$ and $H$ are compatibly almost opposable graphs, then their strong product $G \boxtimes H$ is compatibly almost opposable.

results.title: Strong products with a graph that has a universal vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs. If $G$ is almost opposable and $H$ has a universal vertex, that is, a vertex adjacent to every other vertex of $H$, then the strong product $G \boxtimes H$ is almost opposable.

results.title: Cartesian products of compatibly almost opposable graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be compatibly almost opposable graphs. Suppose that for some vertex $u$ of $G$ there are an involutive automorphism $\alpha$ of $G$ and an opposition $f$ of the induced subgraph $G - u$ on the vertices other than $u$ such that $\alpha(x) = f(x)$ for every vertex $x \neq u$. Then the Cartesian product $G \square H$ is compatibly almost opposable.

results.title: Almost opposability of strong grids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ and $n_1, \dots, n_k \ge 1$. Then the $k$-dimensional strong grid $P_{n_1} \boxtimes \cdots \boxtimes P_{n_k}$, the strong product of the paths $P_{n_i}$ on $n_i$ vertices, is almost opposable.

results.title: Opposability of Cartesian grids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k \ge 1$ and $n_1, \dots, n_k \ge 1$, and let $G = P_{n_1} \square \cdots \square P_{n_k}$ be the $k$-dimensional Cartesian grid, the Cartesian product of the paths $P_{n_i}$ on $n_i$ vertices. Then $G$ is almost opposable if and only if at most one of $n_1, \dots, n_k$ is even, and $G$ is opposable if more than one of them is even.

results.title: First player wins Peaceable Kings
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$, the first player wins Snort on the king's graph of the $n \times m$ board (the Peaceable Kings game).

results.title: Snort on the knight's graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$, the second player wins Snort on the knight's graph of the $n \times m$ board (the Peaceable Knights game) if and only if $n$ is even or $m$ is even.

results.title: Second player wins Peaceable Bishops exactly when a side is even
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$, the second player wins Snort on the bishop's graph of the $n \times m$ board (the Peaceable Bishops game) if and only if $n$ or $m$ is even.

results.title: Snort on the rook's graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$, the second player wins Snort on the rook's graph of the $n \times m$ board (the Peaceable Rooks game) if and only if $n$ and $m$ are both even.

results.title: First player wins Peaceable Queens on boards with an odd side
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$ be natural numbers such that $n$ or $m$ is odd. Then the first player wins Snort on the queen's graph of the $n \times m$ board (the Peaceable Queens game).
